title: A+ Core 2 (220-1202) practice exam
note: Original questions written for MyNextCert from the public 220-1202 exam objectives. Not real exam questions.

q.q: A new storage server will hold years of unit records on very large volumes. The admin wants a Windows file system built to detect and repair data corruption on its own. Which one fits?
o: ReFS
Right. The Resilient File System checks data integrity and can repair corruption, and it's made for large server volumes.
ext4
ext4 is the usual Linux file system. Windows can't use it natively.
exFAT
exFAT is a light file system for flash drives. It has no journaling or self-repair.
FAT32
FAT32 has no integrity checking and can't hold a file over 4 GB.

q.q: A station still runs a few Windows 10 PCs. Windows 10 reached end of support on Oct 14, 2025. What is the main risk of keeping them in service?
o: Their licenses are revoked and Windows deactivates
Licenses aren't revoked when support ends.
They will stop booting after the date
Windows 10 still boots and runs. It just isn't patched anymore.
Microsoft deletes their OneDrive data
End of support doesn't touch cloud data.
They stop getting security patches
Right. After end of support (EOL), new flaws stay unpatched, so the PCs become easy targets.

q.q: A Mac user's external drive works on the Mac, but a Windows PC asks to format it when it's plugged in. The drive was set up with the Mac's default file system. What is the cause?
o: The drive is formatted as exFAT
exFAT works on both Windows and macOS. That's why it's used for shared drives.
The drive is formatted as NTFS, which Macs can't use
Macs can read NTFS, and NTFS isn't the Mac default.
Windows can't natively read APFS
Right. APFS is Apple's file system. Windows doesn't read it without extra software, so it offers to format the drive.
The USB port on the PC is USB 2.0
A slower port changes speed, not whether the file system can be read.

q.q: A technician will install Windows 11 on a new 4 TB drive in a UEFI PC. Which partition style must the boot drive use?
o: An extended partition with logical drives
Extended and logical partitions are an MBR workaround.
MBR
MBR tops out at 2 TB and four primary partitions, and Windows 11 doesn't boot from it in UEFI mode.
A dynamic disk with a spanned volume
Dynamic disks join space across disks. You can't install Windows on a spanned volume.
GPT
Right. Windows 11 boots in UEFI mode, which needs GPT. GPT also handles drives over 2 TB.

q.q: A unit is shipping 200 new laptops straight to members' homes. Each laptop should set itself up with unit apps and policies when the member signs in, and no technician touches it. Which install method is this?
o: A clean install from a USB drive
Someone has to boot each laptop from the USB drive.
Zero-touch deployment
Right. Zero-touch (such as Windows Autopilot) sets the device up from the cloud at first sign-in.
A repair installation
A repair install fixes a broken Windows. It doesn't provision new devices.
A multiboot setup
Multiboot puts more than one OS on a PC so you can choose at startup.

q.q: During Windows Setup on a new server, no drives appear on the "Where do you want to install Windows?" screen. The drives are fine in the RAID controller's setup screen. What should the technician do?
o: Use the recovery partition instead of the USB installer
A new server has no recovery partition, and the problem is the missing driver.
Run a quick format from the RAID setup screen
Formatting doesn't help when Setup can't see the controller.
Convert the drives from GPT to MBR
The partition style doesn't hide drives from Setup.
Load the RAID controller's driver
Right. Setup needs a third-party storage driver for some RAID and storage controllers. Load it from a USB drive on that screen.

q.q: A technician will do an in-place upgrade from Windows 10 to Windows 11 on a member's PC. What should they do first?
o: Turn off the TPM so the upgrade isn't blocked
Windows 11 needs TPM 2.0. Turning it off makes the upgrade fail.
Back up the user's data
Right. Upgrades usually keep files, but a failed upgrade can lose them. Back up first, then confirm the hardware meets the requirements.
Convert the disk to a dynamic disk
Dynamic disks have nothing to do with an upgrade.
Delete the recovery partition to free space
The recovery partition helps if the upgrade fails. Keep it.

q.q: A new laptop came with Windows 11 Home. It must join the unit's Active Directory domain and use BitLocker. What is the simplest fix?
o: Install Remote Server Administration Tools
RSAT manages servers from a PC. It doesn't add domain join to Home.
Keep Home and join a workgroup instead
A workgroup isn't a domain, so domain policies and logons won't work.
Upgrade it to Windows 11 Pro
Right. Home can't join a domain and doesn't have full BitLocker. Pro (or higher) has both.
Install the N edition of Windows 11 Home
N editions only remove media apps. They add nothing.

q.q: The Windows 11 upgrade check fails on an older desktop that runs Windows 10 64-bit with 8 GB of RAM. Which TWO missing items most often cause this? (Choose two.)
o: An NVMe SSD
Any 64 GB or larger drive works. NVMe isn't required.
A Wi-Fi 6 adapter
Wi-Fi isn't a Windows 11 requirement.
UEFI with Secure Boot support
Right. Windows 11 needs UEFI firmware that can do Secure Boot. Legacy BIOS mode fails the check.
TPM 2.0
Right. Windows 11 requires a Trusted Platform Module 2.0 chip, which older boards may lack or have turned off.
A graphics card with 4 GB of VRAM
Windows 11 needs a DirectX 12 capable GPU, but not 4 GB of dedicated VRAM.

q.q: An office overseas bought Windows 11 Pro N licenses. Users say video files won't play in the built-in apps. Why?
o: Pro editions don't include media apps
Regular Pro includes media apps. The N version is the difference.
N editions ship without the media features
Right. N editions leave out media playback apps and codecs. Installing the Media Feature Pack adds them back.
N editions block video for security reasons
It's about included media apps, not security.
The licenses haven't been activated
An unactivated copy still plays video.

q.q: A PC's hard drive light never stops. Task Manager shows one process using the disk heavily, but the technician needs to see which files it is reading and writing. Which tool shows that?
o: Resource Monitor (resmon)
Right. Resource Monitor's Disk tab lists the exact files each process is reading and writing, live.
Disk Cleanup (cleanmgr)
Disk Cleanup removes temporary files. It doesn't show what's being read.
System Information (msinfo32)
msinfo32 shows hardware and system details, not live file activity.
Defragment and Optimize Drives (dfrgui)
dfrgui optimizes drives. It doesn't show which files are in use.

q.q: A user's PC slows to a crawl at 1400 every day. The technician suspects a job that a vendor set up to run daily. Where can they see the job and turn it off?
o: Task Scheduler (taskschd.msc)
Right. Task Scheduler lists every scheduled job with its trigger, and you can disable it there.
Certificate Manager (certmgr.msc)
certmgr manages certificates.
Device Manager (devmgmt.msc)
Device Manager handles hardware and drivers.
Event Viewer (eventvwr.msc)
Event Viewer may log that a task ran, but you can't disable the task there.

q.q: A technician must prove a server is too small by recording CPU, memory and disk use every 30 seconds for a full week. Which tool should they use?
o: System Configuration (msconfig)
msconfig controls startup items and boot options.
Task Manager's Performance tab
Task Manager shows about the last minute. It doesn't keep a log.
Performance Monitor with a Data Collector Set
Right. Performance Monitor (perfmon) can log chosen counters on a schedule for days, then graph them.
Resource Monitor
Resource Monitor shows live activity. It doesn't log a week of data.

q.q: After a display driver update, a laptop's docked monitors flicker. The technician wants to undo just that driver update. Which tool should they use?
o: Registry Editor
Editing the registry by hand is risky and isn't how drivers are rolled back.
Device Manager, Roll Back Driver
Right. Roll Back Driver puts back the previous driver for that one device and changes nothing else.
System Restore to last week
System Restore rolls back system files, settings and apps, which is more than needed.
Disk Management
Disk Management works with drives and partitions.

q.q: Several built-in Windows features crash, and the technician suspects damaged system files. Which command checks the protected system files and replaces bad ones?
o: diskpart
diskpart manages disks and partitions.
gpupdate /force
gpupdate reapplies Group Policy.
chkdsk /f
chkdsk fixes file system errors on the disk. It doesn't check Windows system files.
sfc /scannow
Right. System File Checker compares protected system files to known-good copies and repairs them.

q.q: A user says a new Group Policy hasn't reached their PC. The technician wants to list which policies actually applied to the user and the computer. Which command?
o: whoami /groups
whoami shows the user's groups, not which policies applied.
gpresult /r
Right. gpresult /r shows the Group Policy objects applied to the current user and computer.
gpupdate /force
gpupdate reapplies policy. It doesn't report which policies applied.
net user
net user shows or manages user accounts.

q.q: A technician must move a 400 GB share to a new server over a slow link. The copy must keep NTFS permissions and pick up where it left off if the link drops. Which command fits?
o: md
md makes a directory.
robocopy
Right. robocopy can copy security info (/COPYALL) and restart interrupted files (/Z), and it retries on errors.
copy
copy is for simple file copies. It doesn't keep permissions or resume.
format
format erases a volume.

q.q: A user's connection to a remote site is choppy. tracert completes, but the technician wants packet loss for each hop measured over time. Which command?
o: nslookup
nslookup tests DNS name resolution.
pathping
Right. pathping traces the route, then sends many packets to each hop and reports loss per hop.
ping -t
ping -t tests one destination continuously. It doesn't show which hop drops packets.
netstat
netstat lists connections and listening ports.

q.q: A technician needs drive letter S: on a user's PC to point to \\fs01\shared. Which command does this?
o: cd S:\fs01\shared
cd changes directories. It can't create a mapped drive.
hostname fs01
hostname only shows the PC's name.
net use S: \\fs01\shared
Right. net use maps a drive letter to a network share.
net user S: \\fs01\shared
net user manages user accounts, not drives.

q.q: A user gets an email attachment that shows as invoice.pdf, but it is really invoice.pdf.exe. Which setting change helps users spot this?
o: Sound: play a sound when a file opens
Sounds don't reveal a hidden extension.
Ease of Access: turn on high contrast
High contrast changes colors, not file names.
Indexing Options: add the Downloads folder
Indexing speeds up search. It doesn't show extensions.
File Explorer Options: show file extensions
Right. Turning off "Hide extensions for known file types" shows the real .exe ending.

q.q: Windows search misses documents stored in D:\Projects, and searches there are slow. Which setting should the technician change?
o: Privacy settings
Privacy settings control app access to data, not the search index.
Internet Options
Internet Options are for web settings.
Indexing Options
Right. Add D:\Projects to the indexed locations so Windows catalogs its files and contents.
Power Options
Power settings don't change what search covers.

q.q: A docked laptop goes to sleep when the user closes its lid, which drops the monitors. Where is this changed?
o: Devices and Printers
Devices and Printers lists hardware. It doesn't control lid actions.
Time and Language
Time and Language sets clock, region and language.
Power Options
Right. Power Options sets what closing the lid does, separately on battery and when plugged in.
User Accounts
User Accounts manages sign-in accounts.

q.q: A member's laptop joins a hotel's Wi-Fi. Which network profile should Windows use so the laptop isn't visible to other guests?
o: Public
Right. The Public profile turns off network discovery and file sharing on untrusted networks.
Metered
Metered limits data use. It doesn't change discovery or sharing.
Domain
Windows uses Domain only when it reaches the domain controller. You can't pick it.
Private
Private makes the PC discoverable. Use it only on trusted home networks.

q.q: A PC shows the address 169.254.33.10 and can't reach anything off the local network. What does this tell the technician?
o: The PC is on the guest VLAN
Guest VLANs still hand out normal DHCP addresses.
DNS is down, but routing works
DNS problems don't change the PC's IP address.
The PC couldn't reach a DHCP server
Right. 169.254.x.x is APIPA. Windows assigns it to itself when no DHCP server answers.
The PC has a valid static address
Static addresses aren't normally from 169.254.0.0/16.

q.q: A deployed member uses a phone hotspot with a small data plan. Windows keeps downloading large updates over it. What should the technician set?
o: Set a static IP address
Addressing doesn't affect how much data Windows downloads.
Turn off the Windows Firewall
That lowers security and doesn't reduce data use.
Switch the profile to Private
Private changes discovery and sharing, not data use.
Mark the connection as metered
Right. On a metered connection Windows holds back most update downloads and background sync.

q.q: A Mac user wants automatic hourly backups to an external drive, using the tool built into macOS. What should be set up?
o: FileVault
FileVault encrypts the startup disk. It doesn't back up.
Time Machine
Right. Time Machine is macOS's built-in backup. It keeps hourly, daily and weekly snapshots.
Spotlight
Spotlight is search.
Mission Control
Mission Control shows open windows and desktops.

q.q: A unit Mac laptop will hold sensitive files. Which built-in feature encrypts the whole startup disk?
o: FileVault
Right. FileVault is macOS full-disk encryption.
Keychain
Keychain stores passwords and certificates. It doesn't encrypt the disk.
Gatekeeper
Gatekeeper checks which apps may run.
Disk Utility's First Aid
First Aid checks and repairs a disk. It doesn't encrypt it.

q.q: A user downloads a Mac app as a single file. Opening it mounts a volume with the app icon and an arrow to drag it to Applications. What type of file was it?
o: .pkg
.pkg is an installer package that runs a step-by-step installer.
.msi
.msi is a Windows installer package.
.dmg
Right. A .dmg is a disk image. You mount it and drag the .app into /Applications.
.exe
.exe is a Windows program.

q.q: A SOC analyst must find every "Failed password" line in /var/log/auth.log on a Linux server. Which command does this?
o: df /var/log/auth.log
df shows free disk space.
grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log
Right. grep prints the lines that match a pattern. It's a core log-review tool.
ls "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log
ls lists files. It doesn't search inside them.
chown "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log
chown changes who owns a file.

q.q: A script's owner needs read, write and execute. Its group needs read and execute. Everyone else gets nothing. Which command sets this?
o: chmod 640 script.sh
640 gives no one execute, so the script can't run.
chmod 750 script.sh
Right. 7 = rwx (owner), 5 = r-x (group), 0 = --- (others).
chmod 700 script.sh
700 gives the group no access.
chmod 755 script.sh
755 also lets everyone else read and run it.

q.q: On a Linux workstation, a test web server's name must point to 10.0.0.25 without changing DNS. Which file should be edited?
o: /etc/hosts
Right. /etc/hosts maps names to IP addresses on that machine, and it's usually checked before DNS.
/etc/passwd
/etc/passwd lists user accounts.
/etc/fstab
/etc/fstab lists file systems to mount at boot.
/etc/shadow
/etc/shadow holds password hashes.

q.q: A technician on a Fedora (Red Hat family) workstation must install the curl package. Which command should they use?
o: sudo dnf install curl
Right. Fedora and RHEL use the dnf package manager, and installing needs root rights through sudo.
chmod +x curl
chmod changes permissions on a file that already exists.
su curl install
su switches to another user. It doesn't install packages.
sudo apt install curl
apt is for Debian and Ubuntu.

q.q: A required app only comes in a 64-bit version. The PC has a 64-bit CPU but runs 32-bit Windows 10. What must happen?
o: Add more RAM so the app fits
RAM doesn't change the OS architecture.
Clean-install 64-bit Windows
Right. There's no in-place upgrade from 32-bit to 64-bit Windows. Back up the data and do a clean install.
Install the 64-bit app with an in-place upgrade
Windows can't change from 32-bit to 64-bit in place.
Run the app in compatibility mode
Compatibility mode can't run 64-bit code on a 32-bit OS.

q.q: A mapping app needs a GPU with 8 GB of VRAM. The laptop has integrated graphics that share system RAM. What is the right conclusion?
o: A 64-bit OS turns system RAM into VRAM
OS architecture doesn't create VRAM.
Adding 8 GB of system RAM meets the requirement
Shared memory isn't the same as dedicated VRAM.
Requirements only matter for servers
Ignoring requirements leads to crashes or a program that won't start.
It needs a dedicated GPU that meets the spec
Right. Integrated graphics borrow system RAM and won't meet a dedicated-VRAM requirement.

q.q: A 3 GB app must go to 300 PCs at a sector that shares a slow WAN link. What should the technician plan for?
o: The app's color scheme matching Windows
Appearance has nothing to do with deployment impact.
Changing every PC's network profile to Public
The network profile doesn't reduce download size.
Running the installer on each PC at 0800
300 downloads at the start of the day would saturate the link.
The network impact of 300 downloads
Right. Push it after hours or from a local distribution point, so the WAN isn't swamped during work.

q.q: Members want to sign in to the cloud email and file apps with the same username and password as their on-site domain account. What makes this work?
o: A shared mailbox for each member
Shared mailboxes are for teams. They don't sync logins.
Videoconferencing guest access
Guest access lets outside people join meetings.
Mapping a network drive to the cloud
Drive mapping doesn't sync accounts.
Identity synchronization
Right. Identity sync copies on-site directory accounts to the cloud identity service, so both use the same credentials.

q.q: A user's laptop SSD filled up after they synced a large team document library. They still want to see every file in File Explorer. What should the technician turn on?
o: Files On-Demand in the sync client
Right. Files On-Demand shows every file, but only downloads a file when it's opened.
Disk Cleanup on the system drive
Disk Cleanup frees some space, but the sync will fill it again.
Turn off the sync client
Then the user can't see or open the library from File Explorer.
A bigger email mailbox
Mailbox size has nothing to do with synced files.

q.q: A member transfers out, and the unit pays for each cloud office license. What should happen to their license?
o: Delete the tenant and start over
That would wipe the whole unit's data.
Let them keep using it from the new unit
They'd keep access to data they shouldn't see.
Remove it and give it to the next user
Right. Per-user licenses can be reassigned, which saves buying new ones.
Keep it assigned in case they come back
That wastes a paid license.

q.q: A unit moves to a model where every request is checked for identity, device health and need, even from inside the base network. Which concept is this?
o: Implicit trust for domain-joined PCs
That's the old perimeter model.
Zero Trust
Right. Zero Trust never trusts a request just because it comes from inside. Every access is verified.
Single sign-on
SSO cuts down on logins. It doesn't verify every request.
Defense in depth with a strong perimeter firewall
A strong edge still trusts what's inside, which is what Zero Trust rejects.

q.q: The unit wants outgoing email blocked when it contains Social Security numbers. Which control does this?
o: Mobile device management
MDM manages phones and tablets.
Data loss prevention (DLP)
Right. DLP scans outgoing data for patterns like SSNs and blocks or flags it.
An access control list on the router
ACLs filter by address and port, not by what's inside a message.
Least privilege
Least privilege limits rights, but it can't spot SSNs in an email.

q.q: Members log in once to the unit's identity provider, which then vouches for them to several outside web apps by sending signed XML assertions. Which standard is this?
o: SAML
Right. Security Assertion Markup Language passes signed XML assertions from an identity provider to web apps for SSO.
TKIP
TKIP is an old Wi-Fi encryption method.
Kerberos
Kerberos uses tickets inside a domain, not XML assertions to outside web apps.
RADIUS
RADIUS authenticates network access, such as Wi-Fi and VPN.

q.q: A folder's share permission gives Everyone Full Control. Its NTFS permission gives the Supply group Read. What can a Supply member do when opening it over the network?
o: Full Control
The NTFS Read permission still limits them.
Change
Neither permission grants Change to Supply.
Read only
Right. Over the network, Windows applies the more restrictive of the share and NTFS permissions.
Nothing, because the two permissions conflict
They don't cancel out. The more restrictive one wins.

q.q: A user whose account is in the local Administrators group runs an installer and gets a prompt to allow it to make changes. What is this, and why?
o: Defender, because the installer is malware
A UAC prompt isn't a malware alert.
BitLocker, asking to unlock the drive
BitLocker asks for a PIN or recovery key at boot, not for installs.
UAC, so programs run without admin rights until approved
Right. User Account Control runs even admins with standard rights until they approve elevation.
Windows Hello, enrolling the user's face
Windows Hello is a sign-in method.

q.q: On a shared Windows Pro PC, one user wants a single folder encrypted so other users of that PC can't open it. Which feature fits?
o: EFS
Right. Encrypting File System encrypts chosen files or folders, tied to that user's account.
Share permissions
Share permissions only apply over the network.
BitLocker
BitLocker encrypts the whole drive. Anyone who can log in still sees the files.
UAC
UAC controls elevation, not encryption.

q.q: Members want to sign in to their unit laptops with a PIN or face scan tied to that device instead of a long password. Which feature is this?
o: EFS
EFS encrypts files.
A Guest account
Guest accounts are for temporary users and should be disabled.
Windows Hello
Right. Windows Hello uses a device-bound PIN or biometrics to sign in.
Credential Manager
Credential Manager saves passwords for sites and network resources. It isn't a sign-in method.

q.q: A building's Wi-Fi must make each member sign in with their own account, checked by a central server, instead of one shared password. What should be set up?
o: WPA2-Personal with TKIP
TKIP is outdated, and it's still a shared key.
WPA3-Personal with a long passphrase
Personal mode uses one shared passphrase for everyone.
An open network with a captive portal
Open networks aren't encrypted.
WPA3-Enterprise with RADIUS
Right. Enterprise mode sends each user's login to a RADIUS server, so access is per user and can be revoked.

q.q: Which encryption does WPA2 use in place of the older TKIP?
o: SHA-256
SHA-256 is a hash, not a cipher for Wi-Fi traffic.
MD5
MD5 is a hash, not Wi-Fi encryption.
AES
Right. WPA2 uses AES (CCMP), which replaced the weaker TKIP.
RC4
RC4 was used by WEP and inside TKIP. It's broken.

q.q: Network admins log in to routers and switches through a central server that encrypts the whole session and approves each command separately. Which protocol is this?
o: WPA3
WPA3 secures Wi-Fi.
RADIUS
RADIUS encrypts only the password and combines authentication with authorization.
Kerberos
Kerberos is ticket-based domain authentication.
TACACS+
Right. TACACS+ encrypts the entire payload and separates authentication, authorization and accounting, down to each command.

q.q: Domain logons start failing on one PC with a clock-skew error. The domain uses tickets to prove identity. Which protocol is involved?
o: TACACS+
TACACS+ is for device admin logins.
Kerberos
Right. Kerberos tickets carry timestamps, so a clock off by more than about 5 minutes breaks authentication.
TKIP
TKIP is legacy Wi-Fi encryption.
AES
AES is an encryption cipher.

q.q: A PC's fans roar while it sits idle. CPU use stays near 100%, and an unknown process keeps connecting to an outside server on port 3333. What is most likely installed?
o: A cryptominer
Right. Cryptominers burn CPU or GPU to mine coins for an attacker and talk to a mining pool.
Adware
Adware shows ads. It doesn't max out the CPU for hours.
Ransomware
Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment, which would be obvious.
A keylogger
Keyloggers record keystrokes quietly, without heavy CPU use.

q.q: Antivirus can't find anything, but traffic analysis proves a PC is infected. The malware hides its files and processes from Windows itself. What is the most reliable fix?
o: Turn off System Restore and reboot
That's one removal step, not a fix on its own.
Run a quick scan in normal mode
The rootkit hides from scans run inside the infected OS.
Delete the browser cache
This isn't a browser problem.
Wipe the drive and reimage the PC
Right. A rootkit hides inside the OS, so you can't trust the system to clean itself. Reimaging is the safe fix.

q.q: An attack runs PowerShell commands only in memory and leaves no files on disk, so file scanning finds nothing. What kind of malware is this?
o: A Trojan with a dropper file
A dropper writes a file, which file scanning can find.
Fileless malware
Right. Fileless malware lives in memory and abuses built-in tools such as PowerShell, so it dodges file scans.
A boot sector virus
Boot sector viruses live on disk.
A potentially unwanted program (PUP)
PUPs are installed programs, so they are on disk.

q.q: The SOC wants a tool on every endpoint that records process, file and network activity, flags suspicious behavior and lets an analyst isolate a host remotely. What is this?
o: EDR
Right. Endpoint detection and response records endpoint behavior for investigation and can isolate a host.
An email gateway
Email gateways filter mail before it reaches users.
A host-based firewall
A host firewall filters traffic but doesn't record process activity.
A signature antivirus
Classic antivirus matches known files. It doesn't record activity or isolate hosts.

q.q: Members get a text saying "Your package is held. Pay the fee here," with a short link. What is this?
o: Whaling
Whaling targets senior leaders, usually by email.
Smishing
Right. Smishing is phishing by SMS text message.
Vishing
Vishing uses voice calls.
Shoulder surfing
Shoulder surfing is watching someone's screen or keypad.

q.q: The unit's finance clerk gets an urgent email that seems to come from the commanding officer and asks for a funds transfer to a new account today. The sender's domain is one letter off. What is this?
o: A denial of service attack
DoS floods a service. It doesn't ask for transfers.
SQL injection
SQL injection attacks a database through input fields.
Tailgating
Tailgating is following someone through a secure door.
Business email compromise
Right. BEC impersonates a leader or vendor to get money moved. Verify through another channel.

q.q: A visitor carrying boxes walks through a badge-controlled door right behind a member who held it open. Which threat is this?
o: Dumpster diving
Dumpster diving is going through trash for information.
Tailgating
Right. Tailgating gets someone without a badge through a controlled door behind someone who has one.
An evil twin
An evil twin is a fake Wi-Fi access point.
Spoofing
Spoofing fakes an address or identity on a network.

q.q: Members at the exchange see two Wi-Fi networks with the base's exact name. One has a much stronger signal and asks them to re-enter their password. What is the likely threat?
o: Cross-site scripting
XSS injects scripts into websites.
An evil twin access point
Right. An evil twin copies a real SSID to trick users into joining and handing over credentials.
A brute-force attack
Brute force guesses passwords. It doesn't create a fake network.
A supply chain attack
Supply chain attacks compromise a vendor or product.

q.q: A web server log shows someone typing ' OR 1=1 -- into a login form's username field. What were they trying?
o: SQL injection
Right. That input tries to change the database query so the login check is always true.
A denial of service
One crafted login isn't a flood of traffic.
Cross-site scripting
XSS uses script tags to run code in other users' browsers.
An on-path attack
On-path attacks intercept traffic between two parties.

q.q: A technician has confirmed malware symptoms on a recruiting office PC. Following CompTIA's malware removal steps, what comes next?
o: Educate the user
User education is the last step.
Schedule scans and run updates
That comes after remediation.
Disable System Restore
That comes after quarantining.
Quarantine the PC
Right. Disconnect it from the network so the malware can't spread or send data out.

q.q: Why does the malware removal process have you disable System Restore in Windows before cleaning?
o: System Restore uses too much CPU during scans
Performance isn't the reason.
Restore points may hold the malware
Right. Old restore points can contain the infection, and restoring one would bring it back.
Malware can't run while System Restore is off
Turning it off doesn't stop malware from running.
The antivirus won't install while it's on
Antivirus installs fine with System Restore on.

q.q: The malware is gone, scans are scheduled and System Restore is back on with a new restore point. What is the final step?
o: Disable System Restore
That happens before remediation.
Reimage the PC
The PC is already clean. Reimaging isn't the closing step.
Quarantine the PC
Quarantine happens near the start.
Educate the end user
Right. Teach the user how the infection likely happened so it doesn't happen again.

q.q: Someone could boot an office PC from their own USB drive and copy files without logging in to Windows. What stops this?
o: Disabling the Guest account
The attacker never logs in to Windows.
A longer Windows password
Booting another OS skips the Windows login entirely.
A screen lock after 5 minutes
The screen lock doesn't stop booting from USB.
A UEFI password with USB boot turned off
Right. Lock the firmware with a password, and remove USB from the boot order so it can't be changed back.

q.q: A unit is hardening its Windows workstations against password guessing. Which TWO settings help most? (Choose two.)
o: Enabling the Guest account
Guest accounts add an easy way in.
A minimum password length of 14 or more
Right. Longer passwords take far longer to guess or crack.
Showing the last user name at sign-in
That helps attackers by giving them a valid user name.
Account lockout after several failed attempts
Right. Lockout stops an attacker from trying thousands of passwords.
Turning on AutoRun for USB drives
AutoRun is a malware risk and has nothing to do with passwords.

q.q: A user found a USB stick in the parking lot and plugged it in. Which setting would have stopped programs on it from launching by themselves?
o: Disable the screen saver
That makes the PC less secure and doesn't touch USB.
Enable password expiration
Password age doesn't affect USB drives.
Disable AutoRun/AutoPlay
Right. With AutoRun off, nothing on removable media starts automatically.
Turn on Windows Hello
Windows Hello is a sign-in method.

q.q: A unit-owned phone with work email was stolen. The police report is filed and the phone still shows online in MDM. What should the technician do?
o: Wait for the screen lock to protect it
A screen lock slows an attacker, but wiping removes the data.
Use the locator app and go get it back
Tracking a thief yourself is unsafe, and the data stays exposed.
Change the office Wi-Fi password
That doesn't protect the data on the phone.
Send a remote wipe through MDM
Right. A confirmed theft of a corporate device calls for wiping it before the data can be pulled off.

q.q: Members use their own phones for work (BYOD). The unit must control work apps and data without touching personal photos. What is the usual approach?
o: Banning screen locks to save time
Screen locks are a basic requirement.
Rooting each phone for better control
Rooting breaks the phone's security.
A managed work profile
Right. MDM can manage a separate work profile, so IT can wipe only the work side.
A full device wipe policy on every phone
Full wipes would erase members' personal data.

q.q: IT needs to push Wi-Fi settings, VPN settings and a 6-digit passcode rule to 150 unit iPhones at once. What does MDM use to do this?
o: A content filter
Content filters block web categories.
A locator app
Locator apps find devices. They don't push settings.
A configuration profile
Right. Configuration profiles bundle settings and policies that MDM installs on many devices.
A remote backup
Backups save data. They don't configure devices.

q.q: A technician plans to degauss a box of failed SSDs before disposal. What is the problem?
o: Degaussing makes SSDs catch fire
That isn't the issue.
SSDs must be reformatted before degaussing
Formatting first changes nothing.
Degaussing takes too long for SSDs
It's not about time. It just doesn't work on flash.
Degaussing doesn't erase flash storage
Right. SSDs store data in flash chips, not magnetic platters. Shred or crush them instead.

q.q: Old office laptops will be given to another unit. The drives must be reused, but the old data must not be recoverable. What should the technician do?
o: Delete the user profiles and empty the Recycle Bin
Deleted files are easy to recover.
Overwrite the drives with a secure-erase tool
Right. Wiping overwrites the data so the drives can be reused safely.
Degauss the drives, then reuse them
Degaussing destroys hard drives, so they can't be reused.
A standard quick format
A quick format only resets the file system. The data can still be recovered.

q.q: The unit hires a vendor to shred 300 old hard drives off-site. What should the unit get back to prove it was done?
o: A copy of the vendor's EULA
A EULA is a software license.
A chain of custody form for evidence
Chain of custody tracks evidence for an investigation.
The drives' warranty cards
Warranty cards don't prove destruction.
A certificate of destruction
Right. The certificate records which drives were destroyed, how and when.

q.q: A SOHO router has UPnP turned on. Why do many security guides say to turn it off?
o: Devices can open router ports without approval
Right. UPnP lets any device, including malware, open inbound ports on its own.
UPnP reveals the admin password
UPnP doesn't expose the admin password.
UPnP slows the router's Wi-Fi
Speed isn't the concern.
UPnP turns off WPA3
UPnP doesn't change Wi-Fi encryption.

q.q: A recruiting office has live network wall jacks in the public waiting area that nobody uses. What should be done?
o: Disable those switch ports
Right. Turning off unused ports keeps strangers from plugging in.
Change the SSID
The SSID is for Wi-Fi, not wired jacks.
Set up port forwarding to the jacks
Port forwarding lets internet traffic in. It doesn't secure jacks.
Turn off SSID broadcast
SSID broadcast has nothing to do with wired ports.

q.q: Visitors at a small office need internet only, with no way to reach the office PCs or printer. What should be set up on the SOHO router?
o: DMZ for every visitor device
A DMZ host exposes a device to the internet.
A guest network isolated from the LAN
Right. A guest network gives internet access but blocks the internal network.
IP filtering that allows every visitor
That still puts visitors on the internal LAN.
The office Wi-Fi password written on the wall
That puts visitors on the internal network.

q.q: A vendor posts a SHA-256 value next to its installer download. How does a technician use it?
o: Use it as the installer's license key
A hash isn't a license key.
Hash the file and compare the values
Right. If the hashes match, the file wasn't changed or corrupted in transit.
Use it to confirm the site's certificate
Certificates are checked by the browser, not by a file hash.
Type it into the browser to decrypt the file
Hashes don't decrypt anything.

q.q: A user's browser homepage and search engine keep changing to an unknown site, even after the user resets them. What should the technician check first?
o: Installed extensions
Right. A malicious or hijacked extension often changes the homepage and search settings. Remove it.
The monitor's resolution
Display settings aren't the cause.
The pop-up blocker
The pop-up blocker doesn't reset the homepage.
Private browsing mode
Private mode doesn't change saved settings.

q.q: A member thinks private (incognito) browsing hides their browsing from the unit's network. What does private browsing actually do?
o: Doesn't keep history or cookies on that device
Right. Private mode only skips saving local history, cookies and form data. The network can still see the traffic.
Blocks the unit's web proxy logs
The proxy still logs the requests.
Encrypts all traffic like a VPN
Private mode doesn't encrypt or route traffic differently.
Hides the PC's IP address from websites
Sites still see the same IP address.

q.q: A user's PC takes 6 minutes to become usable after logging in. Task Manager shows a dozen apps set to start with Windows. What should the technician do first?
o: Schedule chkdsk /r to run at the next boot
chkdsk checks the disk for errors. It doesn't trim startup apps.
Increase the size of the paging file
A bigger paging file doesn't stop a dozen apps from loading at sign-in.
Disable unneeded apps in the Startup tab
Right. Too many startup apps slow sign-in. Turning off the ones the user doesn't need is quick and safe.
Run a full in-place repair install of Windows
A repair install is far too drastic for a crowded startup list.

q.q: After a technician plugs a webcam, headset and two drives into a USB hub, Windows says "Not enough USB controller resources." What is the best fix?
o: Update the BIOS to the newest version
Firmware updates rarely add controller resources.
Run sfc /scannow to repair the USB drivers
System files aren't the problem. The controller is out of endpoints.
Move some devices to ports on another controller
Right. Each USB controller has limited endpoints. Spreading devices across controllers clears the warning.
Reinstall the webcam's software and reboot
The software doesn't use controller endpoints. The device does.

q.q: A desktop started getting random blue screens with different stop codes right after a RAM upgrade. What should the technician run?
o: Windows Memory Diagnostic
Right. Random stop codes after a RAM change point to bad or mismatched memory, which the memory test checks.
Disk Cleanup
Temporary files don't cause random stop codes.
gpupdate /force
Group Policy has nothing to do with this.
System Configuration's Startup tab
Startup apps don't cause random stop codes right after a RAM change.

q.q: Over three days, one app's memory use climbs from 300 MB to 9 GB until Windows warns of low memory and apps crash. Restarting the app fixes it for a while. What is the likely cause?
o: A failing hard drive
A bad drive causes read errors, not one process growing.
Too little virtual memory for normal use
The real issue is the app's ever-growing use.
A DNS misconfiguration
DNS has nothing to do with memory use.
A memory leak in that app
Right. A leak never gives back the memory it used. Update or patch the app, and restart it until fixed.

q.q: A PC shuts off by itself a few times a day. Event Viewer logs Kernel-Power event 41, and the case vents are clogged with dust. What should the technician check first?
o: Cooling and overheating
Right. Heat buildup triggers protective shutdowns. Clean the vents and fans, then check temperatures.
The time zone setting
Clock settings don't shut a PC down.
The user's mapped drives
Mapped drives don't cause sudden power loss.
The browser's extensions
Extensions can't cut the power.

q.q: Members with roaming profiles wait several minutes at every sign-in. Their profiles hold years of files on the Desktop and in Documents. What fixes this best?
o: Give each member a local admin account
Admin rights don't shrink the profile.
Redirect those folders to a network share
Right. Folder redirection keeps big folders on the server, so they don't copy down at every sign-in.
Shorten the DHCP lease time
DHCP leases don't affect profile loading.
Turn off the Windows Firewall
The firewall isn't slowing the profile copy.

q.q: A unit's scheduling app crashes the moment it opens after its latest update. Other apps work. What should the technician try first?
o: Clear the app's cache, then reinstall if needed
Right. Bad cached data after an update often crashes an app. Clearing or reinstalling it is the quick fix.
Turn on developer mode to see the crash log
Developer mode adds risk and doesn't fix the app.
Factory reset the phone and restore from backup
A reset wipes everything for a problem in one app.
Roll the whole phone back to the previous OS
Phones generally can't roll back the OS, and the OS isn't the problem.

q.q: Since an OS update, a phone's battery drops from full to empty by noon. What should the technician check first?
o: Replace the battery under warranty
A battery that was fine until the update isn't likely worn out. Check what's using it first.
Battery usage by app in Settings
Right. The battery screen shows which app is draining power, often one stuck running in the background.
Factory reset the phone right away
A reset is a last resort before you know the cause.
Recalibrate the battery by draining it
Calibration fixes wrong percentage readings, not real drain.

q.q: A tablet's screen no longer turns when the user rotates it. What should be checked first?
o: The rotation lock setting
Right. Rotation lock, often turned on by accident from the quick settings, stops autorotate.
The tablet's MDM enrollment
Enrollment doesn't usually lock rotation.
The digitizer cable
The digitizer handles touch, not rotation.
The Wi-Fi band
Wi-Fi has nothing to do with rotation.

q.q: A phone's OS update fails every night with a generic error. The phone has 1.2 GB free and is plugged in. What is the most likely cause?
o: The phone's case is too thick
The case doesn't affect updates.
The screen brightness is low
Brightness doesn't affect updates.
Bluetooth is turned on
Bluetooth doesn't block updates.
Not enough free storage
Right. Updates need space to download and unpack. Free up storage and try again.

q.q: A member's phone won't pay at the exchange's tap terminal, but the same card works when inserted. What should the technician check first?
o: That Bluetooth is paired with the terminal
Tap-to-pay uses NFC, not Bluetooth pairing.
That NFC is on and the wallet card is set
Right. Tap-to-pay needs NFC turned on and a card set up in the wallet app.
That the phone is on the exchange's Wi-Fi network
NFC payments don't need Wi-Fi.
That location services are turned off for the wallet app
Location settings don't block NFC payments.

q.q: A phone restarts on its own several times a day, ever since the user installed a few new apps. What should the technician do?
o: Turn off automatic OS updates
The reboots started with new apps, not an OS update.
Replace the battery, since it can't hold a load
The reboots started with the new apps, so test those first.
Boot to safe mode and remove the new apps
Right. Safe mode loads without third-party apps. If reboots stop, remove the new apps one by one.
Factory reset the phone right away
A reset is a last resort when a safe-mode test can find the cause.

q.q: MDM flags a member's work phone as jailbroken and blocks it from unit email. Why does jailbreaking matter for security?
o: It stops the phone from receiving MDM profiles
MDM can still reach it. The risk is what the jailbreak itself allows.
It only voids the warranty, which breaks policy
The warranty is the least of it.
It turns off the phone's device encryption
Jailbreaking doesn't simply turn off encryption. It breaks the OS's protections.
It removes the OS's built-in security controls
Right. Jailbreaking or rooting bypasses app sandboxing and lets unvetted code run with high privileges.

q.q: A phone's data use jumped from 2 GB to 30 GB this month, though the user's habits haven't changed. A new flashlight app runs all the time. What is the likely cause?
o: Automatic OS updates over cellular
An OS update is a few GB at most, not 28 GB.
Wi-Fi calling routing calls over cellular
Wi-Fi calling uses Wi-Fi, not cellular data.
A malicious app sending data out
Right. A simple app moving lots of data in the background points to malware leaking data.
The carrier changed how it counts data
Billing changes don't explain one app running all the time.

q.q: While browsing, a phone shows a flashing "Your phone has 5 viruses! Install CleanerPro now" page. What should the user do?
o: Close the page without tapping it
Right. Fake warnings push you to install junk or malware. Close the tab and clear browsing data if it keeps coming back.
Install the app it recommends
The "cleaner" is usually the malware.
Give the page permission for notifications
That lets it spam more fake alerts.
Call the phone number on the page
That's a tech support scam.

q.q: An Android work phone has an app the user installed from a website, not the app store. Which setting allowed this?
o: Developer options
Developer options add debug settings, but sideloading is allowed by Install unknown apps.
Default apps
Default apps sets which app opens links and files.
Google Play Protect
Play Protect scans apps. It warns about sideloaded apps; it doesn't allow them.
Install unknown apps
Right. Android blocks apps from outside the store unless an app is allowed to install unknown apps.

q.q: During a check of unit phones, the technician finds USB debugging turned on in developer options on several of them. What is the right action?
o: Turn off developer mode and USB debugging
Right. USB debugging lets a connected computer get deep access to the phone, so it should be off on work devices.
Leave it on, since only IT uses USB cables
Anyone with a cable and a computer could use it.
Factory reset every phone that has it on
Turning the setting off is enough unless something else is wrong.
Install a second antivirus app on each phone
The open setting is the problem, not missing antivirus.

q.q: A member searched the app store for the unit's credit union app and installed one with nearly the same name and logo. It asked for their login and has crashed ever since. What happened?
o: Their data plan ran out
Running out of data doesn't make an app ask for logins.
They installed a spoofed app
Right. App spoofing copies a real app's name and look to steal logins. Remove it and change the password.
The phone's NFC is turned off
NFC isn't involved.
The real app needs an update
The real app wouldn't steal the login.

q.q: Every search in a user's browser lands on an unfamiliar search site, and their bank's address opens a look-alike page. Which file should the technician check for tampering?
o: The Windows paging file
The paging file is virtual memory.
The hosts file
Right. Malware adds lines to the hosts file to send real site names to attacker IPs.
The Recycle Bin
Deleted files don't change name resolution.
The printer spool folder
Print jobs don't redirect websites.

q.q: A pop-up from "PC Defender Pro," which the user never installed, says 47 threats were found and asks for payment to clean them. What is this?
o: A pending Windows Update
Updates don't ask for payment.
A certificate warning
Certificate warnings come from the browser about a site's identity.
A real Windows Defender alert
Defender doesn't charge to remove threats.
Rogue antivirus (scareware)
Right. Fake security alerts scare users into paying or installing malware.

q.q: A user sees certificate warnings on every HTTPS site, even major ones. The PC's date and time are correct. What should the technician suspect?
o: A weak Wi-Fi signal
Signal strength doesn't cause certificate errors.
All of those websites let their certificates expire
Major sites don't all expire at once.
A full Recycle Bin
That has no effect on certificates.
A rogue root certificate or intercepting proxy
Right. With the clock fine, warnings on every site point to something intercepting HTTPS, often malware or an unapproved proxy.

q.q: A user's files now end in .locked and won't open, and a ransom note is on the desktop. What should the technician do first?
o: Restart the PC and keep working
That may let it spread further.
Pay the ransom to get the files back
Paying doesn't guarantee the files come back, and it funds the attackers.
Disconnect the PC from the network
Right. Isolate it first so the ransomware can't encrypt shared drives or spread.
Rename the files to remove .locked
The files are encrypted. Renaming them doesn't decrypt them.

q.q: On a user's PC, Windows Update fails, the antivirus can't download definitions, and the security vendors' websites won't load. Other sites work. What does this pattern suggest?
o: The monitor driver is out of date
Display drivers don't block websites.
The ISP is down
Other sites still load.
The PC's power plan is set to Balanced
Power plans don't block websites.
Malware is blocking security updates
Right. Malware often blocks security sites and updates to protect itself.

q.q: Windows shows a desktop alert that real-time protection was turned off, but the user says they didn't do it. What should the technician do?
o: Reinstall the antivirus and change nothing else
If malware turned it off, it can do it again.
Investigate for malware, then turn protection back on
Right. Malware often turns off antivirus first. Treat an unexplained change as a sign of infection.
Turn off the notification so it stops showing
Hiding the alert hides the problem.
Ignore it, since Windows does this after updates
Unexplained protection changes shouldn't be ignored.

q.q: A user says files in their Documents folder were renamed or are missing, and they didn't touch them. No other users share the PC. What should the technician suspect first?
o: Windows Search re-indexing the folder
Indexing reads files. It doesn't rename or delete them.
A failing monitor cable
Display problems can't change files.
OneDrive Files On-Demand freeing up space
Files On-Demand keeps files listed. It doesn't rename them.
Malware that changes or deletes files
Right. Files changed or missing without explanation are a common malware symptom. Scan the PC and check backups.

q.q: The help desk must respond to priority 2 tickets within 4 hours. Which document sets that promise?
o: The end-user license agreement
A EULA covers software license terms.
The service level agreement (SLA)
Right. An SLA defines the service levels, such as response and fix times, that support agrees to meet.
The incident report
An incident report documents an event after it happens.
The acceptable use policy
An AUP says how users may use systems.

q.q: A technician found the fix for an error that keeps coming back across the unit. Where should they record it so others can solve it faster next time?
o: A sticky note on the server rack
Notes get lost and can't be searched.
A knowledge base article
Right. A knowledge base stores proven fixes so anyone can reuse them.
The asset tag database
Asset records track hardware, not fixes.
Only the ticket's private notes
Others won't find a fix buried in one ticket.

q.q: A switch will be replaced this weekend. Which source shows the servers and services that depend on it, so the change can be planned?
o: The warranty card for the switch
A warranty says what's covered, not what depends on the switch.
The user's email signature
That has nothing to do with dependencies.
The SLA
An SLA sets service targets, not dependencies.
The configuration management database (CMDB)
Right. A CMDB records configuration items and how they relate, including dependencies.

q.q: A member is leaving the unit. Which document makes sure their accounts are disabled, their laptop and tokens are returned and their access is removed?
o: An off-boarding checklist
Right. An off-boarding checklist makes sure nothing is missed when someone leaves.
A purchase order
A PO is for buying things.
A change request form
Change requests cover system changes, not people leaving.
An onboarding checklist
Onboarding covers new arrivals.

q.q: The change board rejects a firewall change request because it doesn't say how to return to the old setup if something breaks. What is missing?
o: A knowledge base article
KB articles document fixes. They aren't part of the change approval.
A rollback plan
Right. A rollback plan explains how to undo the change quickly if it fails.
A purchase approval
Nothing is being bought.
End-user acceptance
User acceptance comes after the change is in place.

q.q: A patch for a flaw that attackers are actively exploiting must go on today, outside the normal weekly change board meeting. Which change type is this?
o: Emergency change
Right. Emergency changes get a fast-track approval for urgent fixes and are reviewed afterward.
Standard change
Standard changes are pre-approved, low-risk routine tasks.
Normal change
Normal changes wait for the regular change board.
Change freeze
A freeze stops changes. It isn't a change type.

q.q: Before an update goes to 400 PCs, the team installs it on copies of the standard PC image in an isolated lab. What is this step called?
o: Peer review of the ticket
Peer review checks the plan. It doesn't test the update.
Risk acceptance
Risk acceptance is a decision, not testing.
Sandbox testing
Right. Testing in an isolated environment finds problems before they reach production.
A maintenance window
A maintenance window is when the change goes live.

q.q: Which plan meets the 3-2-1 backup rule?
o: 3 backups a day, 2 admins, 1 server
That isn't the rule.
3 copies, 2 media types, 1 offsite
Right. Three copies of the data, on two different kinds of media, with one copy offsite.
3 offsite copies on 2 clouds, none on site
The rule keeps copies on site too, for fast restores.
3 full backups, 2 differentials, 1 incremental
The rule is about copies and locations, not backup types.

q.q: A station's backups have reported success every night for a year, but no one has ever restored from them. What should the technician do?
o: Switch to weekly backups
That makes data loss worse.
Delete the oldest backups
That reduces your recovery options.
Trust the success reports
Success messages don't prove the data can be restored.
Run a test restore
Right. A backup isn't proven until you restore from it. Test restores regularly.

q.q: A backup plan keeps daily backups for a week, weekly backups for a month and monthly backups for a year. What is this rotation called?
o: Synthetic full
A synthetic full is built from earlier backups. It isn't a rotation scheme.
The 3-2-1 rule
3-2-1 is about copies, media and location.
In-place recovery
In-place recovery restores to the original location.
Grandfather-father-son (GFS)
Right. GFS keeps daily (son), weekly (father) and monthly (grandfather) sets.

q.q: A desktop's power supply fan has stopped, and the PSU smells hot. What should the technician do?
o: Tape a case fan to the PSU vent
That's unsafe and doesn't fix the failing unit.
Replace the whole power supply
Right. PSUs hold dangerous charge even when unplugged. Swap the unit; don't open it.
Keep using it until it fails
A failing PSU can damage parts or start a fire.
Open the PSU and replace the fan
Capacitors inside can hold a deadly charge.

q.q: An electrical fire starts in a server rack. Which extinguisher is right in the US?
o: Class K
Class K is for kitchen grease fires.
Class C (such as CO2)
Right. Class C is for energized electrical equipment. CO2 leaves no residue.
Class D
Class D is for burning metals.
Class A water extinguisher
Water conducts electricity and can shock the user.

q.q: A technician must move a 40 kg rack UPS alone. What is the safe approach?
o: Drag it by the power cord
That damages the cord and is unsafe.
Lift it quickly with a bent back
That's how back injuries happen.
Leave it plugged in while moving it
Disconnect it first.
Get help or a cart, and lift with the legs
Right. Heavy loads need a second person or equipment. Bend at the knees and keep the back straight.

q.q: A technician needs to know how to safely clean up spilled toner and dispose of a chemical cleaner. Where is this information?
o: The safety data sheet (SDS/MSDS)
Right. The SDS lists hazards, handling, spill cleanup and disposal steps for a product.
The SLA
SLAs set support targets.
The acceptable use policy
The AUP covers how systems may be used.
The printer's warranty
Warranties cover repairs, not chemical safety.

q.q: In winter, a server room's humidity drops to 15%, and technicians feel static shocks touching racks. What is the risk?
o: Condensation on the servers
Condensation comes from too much humidity, not too little.
Faster hard drive wear from moisture
Low humidity means less moisture.
Less need for cooling
Low humidity doesn't change the heat load.
ESD damage to components
Right. Dry air builds static that can damage electronics. Keep humidity in a moderate range.

q.q: A remote station loses power for a few seconds several times a week, and the network switch reboots each time. What should be added?
o: A power strip
A plain power strip only adds outlets.
A UPS
Right. An uninterruptible power supply keeps gear running through short outages and brownouts.
A static mat
Static mats protect parts during repairs.
A surge suppressor
A surge protector blocks spikes. It can't power gear during an outage.

q.q: A laptop is taken as evidence for an investigation. Every person who handles it must sign a log with the date, time and reason. What is this log?
o: An incident ticket
A ticket tracks the work, not the evidence handling.
A chain of custody
Right. The chain of custody proves who had the evidence and when, so it holds up later.
A change request
Change requests cover system changes.
An asset inventory
An inventory tracks equipment you own.

q.q: A responder is collecting data from a running compromised PC. Following the order of volatility, what should be collected first?
o: The hard drive image
Disk data survives a shutdown, so it comes after RAM.
Printed reports
Paper is the least volatile.
Backups from last month
Backups don't change and can be collected any time.
The contents of RAM
Right. Memory disappears when the PC powers off, so it's collected before disk data.

q.q: A unit bought a 50-seat license for drawing software but installed it on 80 PCs. What is the issue?
o: A DRM protection error
DRM controls use of content. The problem here is the unit's own over-install.
A licensing violation
Right. Installing beyond the seats bought breaks the license agreement.
An open-source license conflict
This is commercial software.
A PII exposure
No personal data is involved.

q.q: A technician fixing a yeoman's PC sees a spreadsheet of members' names, SSNs and home addresses on the screen. How should this data be treated?
o: As PII, protected and not shared
Right. Personally identifiable information must be protected under privacy rules. Don't copy or discuss it.
As open-source data anyone may reuse
Open-source is a software license idea.
As public, since it's on a unit PC
Being on a unit PC doesn't make personal data public.
As trash to delete right away
It isn't the technician's data to delete.

q.q: A frustrated user starts yelling that IT never fixes anything. What should the technician do?
o: Raise their voice to match the user
That escalates the situation.
Stay calm, listen and keep to the problem
Right. Don't argue or take it personally. Let them explain, then focus on fixing the issue.
Post about the user on social media
That's unprofessional and breaks confidentiality.
Tell the user to calm down or lose support
Threats make things worse.

q.q: A part for a member's laptop is back-ordered, and the promised fix date will be missed. What should the technician do?
o: Promise a fix tomorrow anyway
Making a promise you can't keep makes things worse.
Close the ticket and open a new one later
That hides the problem and breaks tracking.
Say nothing until the part arrives
Silence damages trust.
Tell the member now and give options
Right. Set clear expectations: give the new timeline and offer a loaner or workaround.

q.q: While fixing a printer at a desk, a technician sees a member's personal medical letter on the desk. What is the professional action?
o: Take a photo for the ticket
Photographing personal documents is never appropriate.
Ignore it and keep it confidential
Right. Don't read, move or mention personal documents you happen to see.
Read it to check it isn't classified
That invades the member's privacy.
Mention it to the member's coworkers
That breaks confidentiality.

q.q: A technician writes a script that maps drives using PowerShell commands. Which file extension should it have?
o: .ps1
Right. PowerShell scripts use .ps1.
.vbs
.vbs is VBScript.
.bat
.bat runs classic Command Prompt commands.
.sh
.sh is a Linux shell script.

q.q: A user found a script on a forum that promises to "double your PC's speed" and wants to run it as administrator. What is the main risk?
o: It could hold malware or change system settings
Right. Scripts from unknown sources can install malware or make changes you didn't intend. Review and test them first.
Scripts can't run as administrator
They can, which is part of the danger.
Scripts only work on Linux
Windows runs .bat, .ps1 and .vbs scripts.
It will use too much monitor brightness
Brightness isn't the risk.

q.q: A Linux admin wants a nightly job that copies the /srv/data folder to a backup server. Which kind of script file is the usual choice?
o: A shell script (.sh)
Right. Linux admins usually automate backups with shell scripts run on a schedule.
A batch file (.bat)
.bat files are for Windows.
A VBScript file (.vbs)
VBScript is Windows-only.
A spreadsheet macro
Macros run inside office apps, not as a system job.

q.q: An admin needs an encrypted command-line session to a Linux server. Which tool should they use?
o: FTP
FTP transfers files and isn't encrypted.
RDP
RDP is a graphical desktop session, mainly for Windows.
Telnet
Telnet sends everything, including passwords, in clear text.
SSH
Right. Secure Shell gives an encrypted remote command line, usually on TCP 22.

q.q: A technician must remotely control a Mac's desktop from a Windows PC with a standard tool. Which option fits?
o: SPICE
SPICE is mainly for connecting to virtual machine consoles.
VNC
Right. VNC works across operating systems, and macOS Screen Sharing is VNC-compatible.
SSH only
SSH gives a command line, not the desktop.
WinRM
WinRM runs PowerShell remoting on Windows, not desktop control.

q.q: A small office has RDP on TCP 3389 open straight to the internet so staff can work from home. What is the safer setup?
o: Move RDP to port 3390
Changing the port only hides it a little. Scanners still find it.
Put RDP behind a VPN with MFA
Right. Exposed RDP is a top attack target. Require a VPN with MFA, and close 3389 to the internet.
Turn off the RDP password requirement
That makes access open to anyone.
Allow RDP only during work hours
Attackers can still get in during those hours.

q.q: A managed service provider uses an RMM tool to patch and control all of a small office's PCs. What is the biggest security concern?
o: A breached RMM account controls every PC
Right. RMM has admin reach to every managed device, so protect it with MFA and least privilege.
RMM can't install patches
Patching is one of its main jobs.
RMM uses too much monitor space
That isn't a security issue.
RMM tools only work on Linux
RMM tools manage Windows, macOS and more.

q.q: An AI assistant gives a technician a confident answer with a PowerShell command and a Microsoft article link. Neither one exists. What is this called?
o: A hallucination
Right. AI tools can make up facts, commands or sources that sound real. Check the output before using it.
A buffer overflow
That's a software vulnerability, not an AI error.
Data poisoning
Data poisoning is when an attacker tampers with training data.
Plagiarism
Plagiarism is copying someone else's work without credit.

q.q: A technician wants to paste a ticket with a member's name, SSN and medical notes into a free public AI chatbot to summarize it. What is the problem?
o: Chatbots only accept text in English
Language isn't the issue.
The summary will be too short
Length isn't the concern.
Chatbots can't summarize text
They can. The issue is data privacy.
It sends private data outside the unit
Right. Public AI tools may store or reuse what you enter. Use only approved tools and keep PII out.

q.q: An AI tool that ranks job applicants keeps scoring one group lower because its training data came mostly from past hires of another group. What is this problem called?
o: A DRM issue
DRM controls copying of content.
Bias
Right. AI trained on lopsided data repeats that imbalance in its results.
A hallucination
A hallucination is made-up content, not a skew in rankings.
Data at rest
Data at rest is stored data.

q.scenario: The unit's office router forwards Remote Desktop (RDP, a way to control a PC from far away) to the workstation ws-ops07 so one user can work from home. This morning the user reports a new, unknown account on the PC. Here are lines from the PC's event logs. Mark the lines that show the attack and leave the normal ones alone. Then pick what the log shows.
q.ticket: Ticket 7742: ws-ops07, unknown local account svc_update found. jsmith works from home at 198.51.100.20 and says they were asleep at 2 a.m. Network Level Authentication is off on this PC, so failed RDP logons show as type 10. Event IDs: 4625 failed logon, 4624 successful logon, 4720 account created, 4732 added to a local group.

lines.text: Nov 23 07:54:20 ws-ops07 Security 4625: Failed logon. Account: jsmith, Logon Type: 2, Workstation: WS-OPS07, Reason: Unknown user name or bad password
lines.why: One failed logon at the keyboard (type 2 is a local console logon) at the start of the workday. That is a normal typo.

lines.text: Nov 23 07:54:41 ws-ops07 Security 4624: Successful logon. Account: jsmith, Logon Type: 2, Workstation: WS-OPS07
lines.why: The user retried and got in at the console. Type 2 and the work PC itself make this expected.

lines.text: Nov 23 12:00:05 ws-ops07 Security 4634: An account was logged off. Account: jsmith, Logon Type: 2
lines.why: A normal logoff at lunch. It does not point to a problem.

lines.text: Nov 23 19:05:12 ws-ops07 Security 4624: Successful logon. Account: jsmith, Logon Type: 10 (RemoteInteractive), Source Network Address: 198.51.100.20
lines.why: A remote desktop logon by jsmith from the home address the ticket says jsmith works from, in the evening. This is the normal way this PC is used.

lines.text: Nov 24 02:14:03 ws-ops07 Security 4625: Failed logon. Account: administrator, Logon Type: 10, Source Network Address: 203.0.113.45, Reason: Unknown user name or bad password
lines.why: A failed Remote Desktop logon (type 10) for the well-known administrator name, from an address that is not jsmith's home address. This is the start of a guessing run.

lines.text: Nov 24 02:14:05 ws-ops07 Security 4625: Failed logon. Account: admin, Logon Type: 10, Source Network Address: 203.0.113.45, Reason: Unknown user name or bad password
lines.why: Two seconds later the same address tries another common name. No person types that fast, so a tool is guessing.

lines.text: Nov 24 02:14:08 ws-ops07 Security 4625: Failed logon. Account: jsmith, Logon Type: 10, Source Network Address: 203.0.113.45, Reason: Unknown user name or bad password
lines.why: Now the guess uses jsmith, a real account on this PC (see the console logons), and the source address has not changed.

lines.text: Nov 24 02:14:10 ws-ops07 Security 4625 (summary): 41 more failed logons for jsmith from 203.0.113.45 between 02:14:10 and 02:16:40, Logon Type: 10
lines.why: Dozens of failures in under three minutes from one address is a brute-force run. No account lockout stopped it.

A service account logged on and created svc_update during patching
Outside RDP password guessing got in, then added an admin
A virus spread from the file server through shared folders

That is a brute-force attack (trying many passwords) followed by persistence. Blocking RDP from the Internet and using an account lockout policy would have stopped it.

q.title: Remove malware from a home-office PC
q.scenario: A teleworker's Windows 11 Home laptop redirects searches to odd sites, shows pop-ups, and its antivirus turned itself off. You have approval to clean it. Build the cleanup in the right order. Leave out steps that spread the infection or waste the cleanup.
q.ticket: Ticket 7755: laptop acts hijacked, antivirus off. Cleanup is authorized by the owner and your supervisor.

rules.text: Investigate and confirm the malware symptoms
rules.why: Check that it really is malware, and what kind, before you act. Pop-ups and redirects can have other causes, and the symptoms guide the cleanup.

rules.text: Quarantine the laptop: unplug the cable and turn off Wi-Fi
rules.why: Cutting the network stops the malware from spreading to other PCs and from talking to its controller. Do it right after you confirm the problem.

rules.text: Turn off System Restore on the laptop
rules.why: Old restore points can hold copies of the malware. Turning System Restore off clears them so the scan can remove everything.

rules.text: Update the anti-malware tool, using definitions from a clean computer
rules.why: Old definitions miss new threats. The laptop is cut off from the network, so bring the update on a clean USB drive or read-only disc.

rules.text: Scan and remove in Safe Mode, or from a boot disc
rules.why: Safe Mode loads only the basics, so most malware that hides in normal startup cannot run or defend itself while the scanner works.

rules.text: Schedule regular scans and automatic updates
rules.why: A cleaned PC can be reinfected. Scheduled scans and updates catch the next threat early.

rules.text: Turn System Restore back on and create a fresh restore point
rules.why: Once the PC is clean, turn this safety net back on so a clean restore point exists for future problems.

rules.text: Teach the user how it happened and how to avoid it
rules.why: Training the user on the bad link or download is the last step, and it helps stop a repeat.

rules.text: Copy the user's files to the office file server before cleaning
rules.why: Copying files from an infected PC to the network can spread the malware to the server. If data must be saved, copy it to offline media and scan it before you restore it.

rules.text: Turn System Restore on before scanning so a bad scan can be undone
rules.why: System Restore would keep infected copies the scanner cannot clean. The malware could come back from an old restore point.

rules.text: Delete unfamiliar files from the Windows folder by hand
rules.why: Guessing can remove files Windows needs and leave the real malware behind. Use the anti-malware tool, which knows what is bad.

rules.text: Reconnect Wi-Fi to download the latest definitions before scanning
rules.why: Reconnecting ends the quarantine, so the malware can spread or call its controller again. Bring the definitions on clean media instead.

before.why: Confirm the problem first. Pulling the network, and then everything else, only makes sense once you know it is malware.
Quarantine comes before cleanup work. Cutting the network first keeps the malware from spreading while you turn off System Restore.
System Restore must be off before the scan, or old restore points can bring the malware back.
Update the scanner first. A scan with old definitions can miss the very threat you came for.
Make the restore point only after the PC is clean. Otherwise the new restore point would hold the malware.
Schedule scans after the cleanup. Setting them up before would not remove the infection that is present now.

last.why: Educating the user is the final step once the PC is clean and protected, so the lesson is about a finished job.

q.title: Roll out a new records app version
q.scenario: The unit wants to move 40 office PCs to a new version of its records app. The old version is known to work, and the update changes how data is saved. The vendor released 6.0 last month and nothing is broken today. This unit's change board asks for test results with the request. Build the steps in the order a change process expects. Leave out steps that skip the controls.
q.ticket: Change request CR-2208: records app 5.2 to 6.0 on 40 PCs, planned for the weekend.

rules.text: Fill out a change request: purpose, scope, affected systems and risk
rules.why: The request is the written record. It tells the change board what changes, who it touches and how risky it is, so they can decide.

rules.text: Test version 6.0 in a sandbox (a safe test copy)
rules.why: A sandbox lets you find problems without harming real users. The test results also give the change board facts to approve against.

rules.text: Get approval from the change board
rules.why: Approval means the people who own the risk agree to the change and the date. Nothing goes live without it.

rules.text: Confirm a current backup exists and write a rollback plan
rules.why: If the update breaks the app, the rollback plan and backup let you return to the working version. They must be ready before you change anything.

rules.text: Schedule a maintenance window and tell the users
rules.why: A set time off hours, with users warned, keeps work from being interrupted and avoids surprise outages.

rules.text: Install version 6.0 on the PCs during the window
rules.why: This is the implementation. It happens only after the request, tests, approval, backup and schedule are in place.

rules.text: Ask users to confirm the app works, as end-user acceptance
rules.why: Users know their own work. Their sign-off shows the change did what it was meant to do, and gives a chance to roll back if it did not.

rules.text: Record the result and close the change
rules.why: The final record shows what was done and how it went. It helps with the next change and with audits.

rules.text: Install it on all 40 PCs first, then write the request later
rules.why: Writing the request after the change skips every control. Nobody checked the risk, the backup or the rollback plan.

rules.text: Label it an emergency change so approval can be skipped
rules.why: An emergency change is for an urgent fix, such as a live outage. A planned upgrade is a normal change and must go to the board.

rules.text: Skip the sandbox test because the vendor says it is stable
rules.why: A vendor cannot know your data or setup. The test is your proof that it works in your own environment.

rules.text: Run the update at midday so any problems show up fast
rules.why: Updating during working hours means problems hit users at once and disrupt duty. A maintenance window avoids that.

before.why: The board approves what is written in the request, so it must exist first.
This unit's change board asks for test results with the request, so test before asking for approval.
Approval comes before implementation. Installing without it is an unapproved change.
The backup and rollback plan must be ready before the install, since they are the way back if it fails.
Users need warning and a set window before the install starts, or the update lands in the middle of their work.
Users can only accept a change that has been made.

last.why: Closing the record is the last step, once the change is done and accepted.

q.title: You find stolen-looking records on a PC
q.scenario: While fixing a slow PC at a unit office you open a hidden folder and see what looks like other members' personal records (names and ID numbers) that do not belong on that PC. The user is not in the room. Build the steps in the order a technician should follow. Leave out steps that harm the evidence or break privacy. You are not the investigator, so do not try to prove anything yourself.
q.ticket: Ticket 7790: slow PC, desk 12. Possible policy violation found while working on the ticket.

rules.text: Stop work and leave the PC as it is. Do not browse more files
rules.why: Opening more files, moving or deleting them changes the evidence. Stopping at once protects it and also limits how much private data you see.

rules.text: Write down the time, PC tag, user and exactly what you saw
rules.why: Notes made now are the first incident documentation. They show the PC's state before anyone else touches it.

rules.text: Tell your supervisor, who decides on informing management or law enforcement
rules.why: Management must be told, and they decide whether other people or law enforcement take over. A technician should not decide that alone.

rules.text: When an authorized person says to, make a bit-for-bit copy of the drive
rules.why: A full copy of the drive keeps the data exactly as found (data integrity), so the original can stay untouched while others examine the copy.

rules.text: Lock up the original and record each handoff on a chain of custody form
rules.why: A chain of custody form lists who held the evidence and when. Without it, a court or an investigation may reject the evidence.

rules.text: Delete the folder so the records cannot spread
rules.why: Deleting destroys evidence and can make the matter worse. The records should be preserved for those who investigate.

rules.text: Run antivirus and finish the slow-PC repair as planned
rules.why: Cleaning or repairing the PC changes files and logs. The repair can wait until the investigators say the PC is free.

rules.text: Ask the user's coworkers if they know why the files are there
rules.why: Talking about it spreads private information and can warn the person involved. Only the proper authority should ask questions.

rules.text: Copy the folder to a USB stick to show your supervisor
rules.why: Copying changes access records on the files and spreads private data onto a loose device. Show your supervisor the PC as you found it, or describe it.

before.why: Stop and do not disturb the PC before you report. The person you tell may need it left exactly as found.
Write your notes before the copy so there is a record of the PC's state before anything was done to it.
Report first. The supervisor decides who receives the PC, and only then do you hand it over and start the form.
Copying needs permission from an authorized person, so report first and wait.
